title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
2.1 SLR vs MLR

SLR: In a simple linear regression (SLR) model, we have one response variable \(y\) and one predictor variable \(x\). \[y=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \epsilon\]

For individual \(i\), \(i=1, \ldots, n\), \[y_i= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i\]

MLR: In a multiple linear regression (MLR) model, we have one response variable \(t\) and multiple predictor variables \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_p\). \[y= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots, \beta_p x_p + \epsilon\]

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
2.2 MLR

For indivuidual \(i\), \(i=1, \ldots, n\), \[y_i= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip} + \epsilon_i\] where
\(y_i\) is the response variable for individual \(i\).
\(x_{ij}\) is the value of predictor variable \(j\) for individual \(i\).
\(\epsilon_i\)’s are errors:

The assumptions on \(\epsilon_i\)’s are the same as those in SLR.
weaker version: \(\epsilon_i\)’s are independent with mean 0 and constant variance \(\sigma^2\).
Strong version: \(\epsilon_i\)’s are i.i.d. \(N(0, \sigma^2)\).

The parameters to be estimated are \(\beta_0, \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_p\) and \(\sigma^2\).

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
2.3 Notations

When putting all individuals together, we have \[\begin{align*}
y_1 &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{11} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{1p} + \epsilon_1 \\
y_2 &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{21} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{2p} + \epsilon_2 \\
&\vdots \\
y_n &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{n1} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{np} + \epsilon_n
\end{align*}\]

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
2.4 Matrix Form

In matrix form, we have \[\begin{bmatrix}y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_n\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & x_{11} & x_{12} & \cdots & x_{1p} \\ 1 & x_{21} & x_{22} & \cdots & x_{2p} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 1 & x_{n1} & x_{n2} & \cdots & x_{np}\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \\ \beta_2 \\ \vdots \\ \beta_p\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}\epsilon_1 \\ \epsilon_2 \\ \vdots \\ \epsilon_n\end{bmatrix}\]

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
2.5 Matrix Form
More compactly, \[\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}\]
here

\(\mathbf{y}\) is the response vector of size \(n \times 1\).
\(\mathbf{X}\) is the design matrix of size \(n \times (p+1)\).
\(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is the parameter vector of size \((p+1) \times 1\).
\(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) is the error vector of size \(n \times 1\), where \(E(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \mathbf{0}\) and \(Var(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_n\). Here \(\sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_n\) is the variance covariance of \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) - it is a diagonal matrix with diagonal elements \(\sigma^2\).

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
2.6 Matrix Form

\(\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix}y_1 \\ \vdots \\ y_n\end{bmatrix}\) is the response vector of size \(n \times 1\).
\(\mathbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & x_{11} & x_{12} & \cdots & x_{1p} \\  \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 1 & x_{n1} & x_{n2} & \cdots & x_{np}\end{bmatrix}\) is the design matrix of size \(n \times (p+1)\).
\(\boldsymbol{\beta} = \begin{bmatrix}\beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \\ \vdots \\ \beta_p\end{bmatrix}\) is the parameter vector of size \((p+1) \times 1\).
\(\boldsymbol{\epsilon} = \begin{bmatrix}\epsilon_1 \\ \vdots \\ \epsilon_n\end{bmatrix}\) is the error vector of size \(n \times 1\).

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
3.1 Least Squares Estimation (LSE) for MLR

The least squares estimation (LSE) of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is obtained by minimizing the residual sum of squares (RSS): \[RSS(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - E[y_i])^2 = (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})^T (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta})\] where \(E[y_i] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip}\) is the fitted value for individual \(i\).

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
3.2 LSE for MLR: \(p=2\)

Let’s consider \(p=2\) for illustration: \[RSS(\beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2) = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_{i1} - \beta_2 x_{i2})^2\]
To find the minimum, we take the partial derivatives with respect to \(\beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2\) and set them to zero:

\[\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial RSS}{\partial \beta_0} &= -2 \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_{i1} - \beta_2 x_{i2}) = 0 \\
\frac{\partial RSS}{\partial \beta_1} &= -2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i1} (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_{i1} - \beta_2 x_{i2}) = 0 \\
\frac{\partial RSS}{\partial \beta_2} &= -2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i2} (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_{i1} - \beta_2 x_{i2}) = 0
\end{align*}\]

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
3.3 Normal Equations: \(p=2\)

Note that there are three linear equations. They can be rewritten as: \[\begin{align*}
n \beta_0 + \beta_1 \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i1} + \beta_2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i2} & = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i\\
\beta_0 \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i1} + \beta_1 \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i1}^2 + \beta_2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i1} x_{i2} & = \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i1} y_i\\
\beta_0 \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i2} + \beta_1 \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i1} x_{i2} + \beta_2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i2}^2 & = \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i2} y_i
\end{align*}\]
These equations are called the normal equations.

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
3.4 Normal Equations: \(p=2\)

To connect the normal equations to their matrix form, we can write them as: \[\begin{bmatrix}n & \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i1} & \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i2} \\ \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i1} & \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i1}^2 & \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i1} x_{i2} \\ \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i2} & \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i1} x_{i2} & \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i2}^2\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \\ \beta_2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i \\ \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i1} y_i \\ \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i2} y_i\end{bmatrix}\]

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
3.5 Normal Equations: Matrix Form for \(p=2\)
Recall that

\(\mathbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & x_{11} & x_{12}\\  1 & x_{21} & x_{22}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots\\ 1 & x_{n1} & x_{n2}\end{bmatrix}\) is the design matrix of size \(n \times (p+1)\).
\(\boldsymbol{\beta}= \begin{bmatrix}\beta_0 \\ \beta_1  \\ \beta_2\end{bmatrix}\) is the parameter vector of size \((p+1) \times 1\).
\(\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix}y_1 \\ \vdots \\ y_n\end{bmatrix}\) is the response vector of size \(n \times 1\).
We can verify that the normal equations can be written as: \[\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}\]
How to solve for \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\)?

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
section: 4.1 Normal Equations: Matrix Form for general \(p\)
text:
4.1 Normal Equations: Matrix Form for general \(p\)

For general \(p\), the normal equations can be written as: \[\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}\]
If \(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}\) is invertible, the LSE of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is given by: \[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} =\begin{bmatrix}\hat{\beta}_0 \\ \hat{\beta}_1 \\ \vdots \\ \hat{\beta}_p\end{bmatrix}
=(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}\]

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text: 4.2 Matrix Form Deriviation of LSE

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
4.3 MLR: fitted values

The fitted values can be computed as: \[\hat{\mathbf{y}} =\begin{bmatrix}\hat{y}_1 \\ \hat{y}_2 \\ \vdots \\ \hat{y}_n\end{bmatrix}
=\mathbf{X} \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \mathbf{X} (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}\]
The hat matrix: \[\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X} (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T\]

Note that \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}= \mathbf{H} \mathbf{y}\).

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
5.1 SSE and MSE

The sum of squared errors (SSE) can be computed as: \[\begin{align*}
SSE & = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i -\hat y_i)^2 = \hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}^T \hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} = (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^T (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\\
&=[(\mathbf{I}_n - \mathbf{H}) \mathbf{y}]^T (\mathbf{I}_n - \mathbf{H}) \mathbf{y}\\
&=\mathbf{y}^T (\mathbf{I}_n - \mathbf{H}) \mathbf{y} \\
\end{align*}\]
The mean squared error (MSE) is given by: \[MSE = \frac{SSE}{n-(p+1)}\] where \(n-(p+1)\) is the degrees of freedom (d.f.) for error.
An unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\) is given by \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = MSE\).

6.1 Example: Heights

This is a simulated data set to practice MLR.

library(MASS)
parents <- mvrnorm(n,
  mu    = c(69.1, 63.7),                 
  Sigma = matrix(c(3^2, 0.2*3*2.8,
                   0.2*3*2.8, 2.8^2), 2, 2))

  0.60*midp + sex_eff + rnorm(n, 0, 2.5)

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
7.1 Statistical Inference About Regression Parameters

Under the strong version of the model assumptions, we have: \[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sim N(\boldsymbol{\beta}, \sigma^2 (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1})\]
The variance (var-cov) of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) can be estimated by: \[\widehat{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = s^2 (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1}\]
The standard error (SE) of \(\hat{\beta}_j\) is given by: \[SE(\hat{\beta}_j) = s \sqrt{ \cdot [(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj}}\] where \([(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj}\) is the \(j\)-th diagonal element of the matrix \((\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1}\).

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
7.2 t-tests For Regression Parameters

To test the significance of each predictor variable, we can use the t-test: \[t = \frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \beta_{j0}}{SE(\hat{\beta}_j)}\] where \(\beta_{j0}\) is the hypothesized value of \(\beta_j\) under the null hypothesis.
Under the null hypothesis \(H_0: \beta_j = \beta_{j0}\), the test statistic follows a t-distribution with \(n-(p+1)\) degrees of freedom: \[t \sim t_{n-(p+1)}\]

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
7.3 t-tests For Regression Parameters

We mentioned that \(\hat\beta_j\) follows a normal distribution. To construct a t statistic, we also need the following.
It can be shown that \(\hat\beta_j\) and \(s^2\) are independent, and \[\frac{(n-(p+1))s^2}{\sigma^2} = \frac{SSE}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-(p+1)}\]
Therefore, we have \[\frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \beta_j}{SE(\hat{\beta}_j)} = \frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \beta_j}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 [(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj}}} \bigg/ \sqrt{\frac{(n-(p+1))s^2}{\sigma^2 (n-(p+1))}} \sim t_{n-(p+1)}\]

title: Lec 07: Multiple Linear Regression - Introduction
text:
7.4 Confidence Intervals For Regression Parameters

A \((1-\alpha)100\%\) confidence interval for \(\beta_j\) is given by: \[\hat{\beta}_j \pm t_{\alpha/2, n-(p+1)} \cdot SE(\hat{\beta}_j)\] where \(t_{\alpha/2, n-(p+1)}\) is the \((1-\alpha/2)\) quantile of the t-distribution with \(n-(p+1)\) degrees of freedom.
This confidence is derived from the t-test statistic, as follows: \[\begin{align*}
1-\alpha=P\left(-t_{\alpha/2, n-(p+1)} \leq \frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \beta_j}{SE(\hat{\beta}_j)} \leq t_{\alpha/2, n-(p+1)}\right) &\\
= P\left(\hat{\beta}_j - t_{\alpha/2, n-(p+1)} SE(\hat{\beta}_j) \leq \beta_j \leq \hat{\beta}_j + t_{\alpha/2, n-(p+1)} SE(\hat{\beta}_j)\right)&
\end{align*}\]

title: Lec 05: Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
2.1 Assumptions in SLR

The SLR model is based on several assumptions:

Linearity: The relationship between \(x\) and \(y\) is linear.
Independence: The errors \(\epsilon_i\) are independent. A weaker assumption is that the errors are uncorrelated.
Homo scedas ticity: The errors \(\epsilon_i\) have constant variance \(\sigma^2\).
Normality: The errors \(\epsilon_i\) are normally distributed.

title: Lec 05: Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
2.2 Model Diagnostics in SLR

Violating any of these assumptions can lead to problems with estimation, prediction, and inference.
Visualization is key to check these assumptions, especially plots based on residuals.

4.1 Assumption 2: Autocorrelation of residuals

Residual plot can be used to uncover the potential correlation between errors. A more formal way to examine the assumption is to use so-called autocorrelation plot.



Code
set.seed(1)
n=100
x=seq(1, n)
e=rnorm(n)
for(i in 2:n){
  e[i]=0.7*e[i-1]+rnorm(1, sd=0.5)
}
y=2+3*x/10+e
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
fit=lm(y~x)
## autocorrelation plot
plot(fit, which=1)
acf(fit$residuals, main="ACF of residuals")









Code

In this case, we can use time series or spatial models to account for the correlation.

title: Lec 03: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
text:
1 Intro

1.0.1 Review: Lecture 01

In lecture 01, we introduced the simple linear regression model and the least squares estimation (LSE) method.
LSE: \[\text{SSE} = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \hat\beta_1 x_i)^2\] \[\{\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1\} = \arg\min_{\beta_0, \beta_1} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i -\beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2\]
The LSEs are \[\hat\beta_1 =\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}, \quad \hat\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \hat\beta_1 \bar{x}.\]



1.0.2 Review: Lecture 02

In lecture 02, we discussed distribution, confidence interval, and hypothesis testing related to \(\beta_1\). In particular, we showed that
\[\hat\beta_1 =\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}\]
\(Var(\hat\beta_1)= \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{XX}}\), where \(S_{XX}=\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2\)
\[T=\frac{\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1}{s/\sqrt{S_{xx}}} =\frac{\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1}{se(\hat\beta_1)} \sim t_{n-2}\]

where \(se(\hat{\beta_1}) =\sqrt{\hat{Var}(\hat\beta_1)}= \sqrt{\frac{s^2}{S_{XX}}}\) and \(s^2 = \frac{SSE}{n-2}\).


1.0.3 Outline

In this lecture, we will continue to discuss inference. We will focus on

estimating a mean response
predicting a new response
analysis of variance (ANOVA)





2 Distribution of \(\hat\beta_0\)

2.0.1 Distribution of \(\hat\beta_0\)

Recall the simple linear regression model: \[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i, \quad \epsilon_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2), \quad i=1,2,\ldots,n.\]
The least squares estimator of \(\beta_0\) is \[\hat\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \hat\beta_1 \bar{x}.\]
The expectation of \(\hat\beta_0\) is \[\begin{align*}
  E(\hat\beta_0) &= E(\bar{y} - \hat\beta_1 \bar{x}) \\
  &= E(\bar{y}) - \bar{x} E(\hat\beta_1) \\
  &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \bar{x} - \bar{x} \beta_1 = \beta_0.
\end{align*}\]



2.0.2 Distribution of \(\hat\beta_0\)

\(\hat\beta_0\) is a linear function of \(y_i\)’s: \[\begin{align*}
  \hat\beta_0 &= \bar{y} - \hat\beta_1 \bar{x} \\
  &= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n y_i - \frac{\bar{x}}{S_{XX}} \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x}) y_i \\
  &= \sum_{i=1}^n \left( \frac{1}{n} - \frac{\bar{x}}{S_{XX}} (x_i - \bar{x}) \right) y_i.
\end{align*}\]
Since \(\hat\beta_0\) is a linear combination of \(y_i\)’s, it is normally distributed.
We have already find its mean (the LSE of \(\beta_0\) is unbiased). Next, we will find its variance.



2.0.3 Variance of \(\hat\beta_0\)

The variance of \(\hat\beta_0\) is \[\begin{align*}
   \text{Var}(\hat\beta_0) &= \text{Var}\left( \sum_{i=1}^n \left( \frac{1}{n} - \frac{\bar{x}}{S_{XX}} (x_i - \bar{x}) \right) y_i \right) \\
   &= \sum_{i=1}^n \left( \frac{1}{n} - \frac{\bar{x}}{S_{XX}} (x_i - \bar{x}) \right)^2 \text{Var}(y_i) \\
   &= \sigma^2 \sum_{i=1}^n \left( \frac{1}{n} - \frac{\bar{x}}{S_{XX}} (x_i - \bar{x}) \right)^2.
\end{align*}\]
After some algebra, we have \[\text{Var}(\hat\beta_0) = \sigma^2 \left( \frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{XX}} \right).\]



2.0.4 Distribution of \(\hat\beta_0\)

We have shown that \(\hat\beta_0\) is a linear combination of \(y_i\)’s, so it is normally distributed. We have also found its mean and variance. Therefore, \[\hat\beta_0 \sim N\left( \beta_0, \sigma^2 \left( \frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{XX}} \right) \right).\]
When inference of \(\hat\beta_0\) is needed, we can construct a t-statistic.
The t-statistic for \(\beta_0\) is \[t = \frac{\hat\beta_0 - \beta_0}{s \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{XX}}}} \sim t_{n-2},\] where \(s^2 = \text{SSE}/(n-2)\) is the unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\).
Confidence interval and hypothesis testing for \(\beta_0\) can be conducted based on the above t-statistic.



2.0.5 Variance of \(\hat\beta_0\): Method 2

We present a different way to find \(\text{Var}(\hat\beta_0)\). \[\begin{align*}
  \text{Var}(\hat\beta_0) &= \text{Var}(\bar{y} - \hat\beta_1 \bar{x}) \\
  &= \text{Var}(\bar{y}) + \bar{x}^2 \text{Var}(\hat\beta_1) - 2\bar{x} \text{Cov}(\bar{y}, \hat\beta_1).
\end{align*}\]
Need to find \(\text{Var}(\bar{y})\) and \(\text{Cov}(\bar{y}, \hat\beta_1)\).
Variance of \(\bar{y}\):

\(\text{Var}(\bar{y})=\text{Var}(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i ) = \frac{1}{n^2} n \sigma^2 = \sigma^2/n\)


2.0.6 Covariance of \(\bar{y}\) and \(\hat\beta_1\)



2.0.7 Variance of \(\hat\beta_0\): Method 2
Putting everything together, we have \[\begin{align*}
\text{Var}(\hat\beta_0)
&= \text{Var}(\bar{y}) + \bar{x}^2 \text{Var}(\hat\beta_1) - 2\bar{x} \text{Cov}(\bar{y}, \hat\beta_1) \\
&= \frac{\sigma^2}{n} + \bar{x}^2 \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{XX}} - 2\bar{x} \cdot 0 \\
&= \sigma^2 \left( \frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{XX}} \right).
\end{align*}\] This is the same result as before.



3 Cov(\(\hat\beta_0\), \(\hat\beta_1\))

3.0.1 Covariance of \(\hat\beta_0\) and \(\hat\beta_1\)

In many inference problems, we need the covariance of \(\hat\beta_0\) and \(\hat\beta_1\). With normality assumptions, we can find the joint distribution of \(\hat\beta_0\) and \(\hat\beta_1\).
Covariance of \(\hat\beta_0\) and \(\hat\beta_1\): \[\begin{align*}
\text{Cov}(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)
&= \text{Cov}(\bar y - \hat\beta_1 \bar x,\; \hat\beta_1) \\
&= \text{Cov}(\bar y,\hat\beta_1) - \bar x\,\text{Var}(\hat\beta_1) \\
&= 0 - \bar x \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{XX}} \quad\text{(from previous results)}\\
&= -\frac{\bar x \sigma^2}{S_{XX}}.
\end{align*}\]




4 Mean Response

4.0.1 Mean Response

A common interest in regression analysis is to estimate the mean response at a given value of \(x\), say \(x_h\).
The mean response at \(x_h\) is \[\mu_{y|x_h} = E(y|x=x_h) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_h.\]
The point estimator of \(\mu_{y|x_h}\) is \[\hat\mu_{y|x_h} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_h.\]



4.0.2 Distribution of \(\hat\mu_{y|x_h}\)

Since \(\hat\mu_{y|x_h}\) is a linear combination of \(\hat\beta_0\) and \(\hat\beta_1\), therefore a linear combination of \(y_i\)’s (which are independently normal). Thus, \(\hat\mu_{y|x_h}\) is normally distributed.
The expectation of \(\hat\mu_{y|x_h}\) is \[\begin{align*}
  E(\hat\mu_{y|x_h}) &= E(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_h) \\
  &= E(\hat\beta_0) + x_h E(\hat\beta_1) \\
  &= \beta_0 + x_h \beta_1 = \mu_{y|x_h}.
\end{align*}\]



4.0.3 Distribution of \(\hat\mu_{y|x_h}\)

The variance of \(\hat\mu_{y|x_h}\) is \[\begin{align*}
  \text{Var}(\hat\mu_{y|x_h}) &= \text{Var}(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_h) \\
  &= \text{Var}(\hat\beta_0) + x_h^2 \text{Var}(\hat\beta_1) + 2 x_h \text{Cov}(\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1).
\end{align*}\]
Plugging in the previous results, we have \[\begin{align*}
  \text{Var}(\hat\mu_{y|x_h}) &= \sigma^2 \left( \frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{XX}} \right) + x_h^2 \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{XX}} + 2 x_h \left( -\frac{\bar{x} \sigma^2}{S_{XX}} \right) \\
  &= \sigma^2 \left( \frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_h - \bar{x})^2}{S_{XX}} \right).
\end{align*}\]
Therefore, \[\hat\mu_{y|x_h} \sim N\left( \mu_{y|x_h}, \sigma^2 \left( \frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_h - \bar{x})^2}{S_{XX}} \right) \right).\] 



4.0.4 Confidence Interval for Mean Response

Since \(\hat\mu_{y|x_h}\) is normally distributed, we can construct a t-statistic for \(\mu_{y|x_h}\):

\[t = \frac{\hat\mu_{y|x_h} - \mu_{y|x_h}}{s \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_h - \bar{x})^2}{S_{XX}}}} \sim t_{n-2},\] where \(s^2 = \text{SSE}/(n-2)\) is the unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\).

A \((1-\alpha)100\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu_{y|x_h}\) is \[\hat\mu_{y|x_h} \pm t_{\alpha/2, n-2} \cdot s \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_h - \bar{x})^2}{S_{XX}}},\] where \(t_{\alpha/2, n-2}\) is the \((1-\alpha/2)\) quantile of the \(t\) distribution with \(n-2\) degrees of freedom.

5 Prediction of a New Response

5.0.1 Prediction of a New Response

Another common interest in regression analysis is to predict a new response at a given value of \(x\), say \(x_h\).
The new response at \(x_h\) is \[y_{\text{new}} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_h + \textcolor{red}{\epsilon},\] where \(\epsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\) is independent of the \(\epsilon_i\)’s in the original model.
The point predictor of \(y_{\text{new}}\) is \[\hat{y}_{\text{new}} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_h.\]



5.0.2 Mean and Variance of \(\hat{y}_{\text{new}}\)

Note that \(\hat{y}_{\text{new}}\) is the same as \(\hat\mu_{y|x_h}\), the point estimator of the mean response at \(x_h\).
They have the same mean and variance.
To construct a prediction interval for \(y_{\text{new}}\), we need to account for the extra variability due to \(\epsilon\).
Technically, we need to find the distribution of \[\hat{y}_{\text{new}} - y_{\text{new}}\]



5.0.3 Distribution of \(\hat{y}_{\text{new}} - y_{\text{new}}\)
\[\begin{align*}
\hat{y}_{\text{new}} - y_{\text{new}}
&= (\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_h) - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_h + \epsilon) \\
&= (\hat\beta_0 - \beta_0) + (\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1) x_h - \epsilon.
\end{align*}\]

Mean: \[\begin{align*}
E[\hat{y}_{\text{new}} - y_{\text{new}}]
&= E(\hat\beta_0 - \beta_0) + x_h E(\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1) - E(\epsilon) \\
&= 0 + x_h \cdot 0 - 0 = 0.
\end{align*}\]



5.0.4 Distribution of \(\hat{y}_{\text{new}} - y_{\text{new}}\)

Variance: \[\begin{align*}
Var(\hat{y}_{\text{new}} - y_{\text{new}})
&=  Var(\hat{y}_{\text{new}}) + Var(y_{\text{new}}) + 0\\
&= \sigma^2 \left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_h - \bar{x})^2}{S_{XX}} \right) + \textcolor{red}{\sigma^2}\\
&= \sigma^2 \left(\textcolor{red}{ 1} + \frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_h - \bar{x})^2}{S_{XX}} \right).
\end{align*}\]

The first step is true because \(y_{\text{new}}\) is a new data point, thus is independent of \(\hat\mu_{y|x_h}\), which replies on the old data.


5.0.5 Distribution of \(\hat{y}_{\text{new}} - y_{\text{new}}\)

Note that the variance of \(\hat{y}_{\text{new}} - y_{\text{new}}\) has an extra \(\sigma^2\) term compared to the variance of \(\hat\mu_{y|x_h}\).
This extra \(\sigma^2\) term accounts for the variability of the new observation \(y_{\text{new}}\) due to the random error \(\epsilon\).
We already explained that \(\hat\mu_{y|x_h}\) follows a normal distribution.
\(y_{\text{new}}\) also follows a normal distribution and it is independent of \(\hat\mu_{y|x_h}\) because it is a new data point.



5.0.6 Distribution of \(\hat{y}_{\text{new}} - y_{\text{new}}\)

As a result, \(\hat{y}_{\text{new}} - y_{\text{new}}\) also follows a normal distribution.
The standardized version is \[\frac{\hat{y}_{\text{new}} - y_{\text{new}}}{\sigma\sqrt{\textcolor{red}{1} + \frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_h - \bar x)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)^2}}}\] which follows a standard normal distribution.
But we don’t know \(\sigma\), so we need to estimate it by \(s=\sqrt{\text{SSE}/(n-2)}\).
The resulting distribution is a t-distribution with \(n-2\) degrees of freedom.



5.0.7 Prediction Interval

We explained that \[t = \frac{\hat{Y}_{\text{new}} - Y_{\text{new}}}{s \sqrt{\textcolor{red}{1} + \frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_h - \bar{X})^2}{S_{XX}}}} \sim t_{n-2},\] where \(s^2 = \text{SSE}/(n-2)\) is the unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\).
A \((1-\alpha)100\%\) prediction interval for \(Y_{\text{new}}\) is \[\hat{Y}_{\text{new}} \pm t_{\alpha/2, n-2} \cdot s \sqrt{\textcolor{red}{1} + \frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_h - \bar{X})^2}{S_{XX}}},\] where \(t_{\alpha/2, n-2}\) is the \((1-\alpha/2)\) quantile of the \(t\) distribution with \(n-2\) degrees of freedom.

7 ANOVA in SLR

7.0.1 Sum of Squares Decomposition

Total Sum of Squares (SST): \[SST = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2\]
The total variation in the response variable.
Regression Sum of Squares (SSR): \[SSR = \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2\] The variation explained by the predictor (regression model).
Error Sum of Squares (SSE): \[SSE = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\] The variation not explained by the model (regression).

7.0.3 Decomposition of the Total Sum of Squares
It can be shown that: \[SST = SSR + SSE\]
Proof: \[\begin{align*}
SST &= \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2 \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^n \big[(y_i - \hat{y}_i) + (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})\big]^2 \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2 + 2\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y}) \\
    &= SSE + SSR + 2\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})
\end{align*}\]

7.0.4 ANOVA Table for SLR
An analysis of variance (ANOVA) table summarizes the results of the regression analysis. - SSTO is decomposed to SSR and SSE. - An F-test is used for assessing whether there is a linear trend between \(x\) and \(y\):
\(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) vs. \(H_a: \beta_1 \neq 0\).

\(R^2\) can be computed from the table. (how?)

[
\[\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\textbf{Source} & \textbf{DF} & \textbf{SS} & \textbf{MS} & \textbf{F} \\
\hline
Regression & 1 & SSR & MSR = SSR/1 & F = MSR/MSE \\
Error      & n-2 & SSE & MSE = SSE/(n-2) & \\
Total      & n-1 & SST & & \\
\hline
\end{array}\]
]


7.0.5 ANOVA Table for SLR

DF: degrees of freedom
SS: sum of squares
MS: mean square (SS divided by corresponding DF)
F: F-statistic for testing \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) vs. \(H_a: \beta_1 \neq 0\)
Under \(H_0\), \(F \sim F_{1, n-2}\).



7.0.6 Expected Mean Squares

We will rewrite SSR in terms of \(\hat\beta_1\):

\[\begin{align*}
SSR &= \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2 \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 X_i - \bar{y})^2 \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat\beta_1 (X_i - \bar{X}))^2 \quad\text{(since $\hat\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \hat\beta_1 \bar{X}$)}\\
    &= \hat\beta_1^2 \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2 = \hat\beta_1^2 S_{XX}.
\end{align*}\] - Therefore, \[MSR = SSR/1 = \hat\beta_1^2 S_{XX}.\]


7.0.7 Expected Mean Squares

We find that \(SSR=\hat\beta_1^2 S_{XX}\). But \(\hat\beta_1 \sim N(\beta_1, \sigma^2/S_{XX})\). Note that \(Var(\hat\beta_1) = E(\hat\beta_1^2) - E^2[\hat\beta_1]\). Therefore, \[\begin{align*}
E[SSR] &= E[\hat\beta_1^2 S_{XX}] \\
     &= S_{XX} E[\hat\beta_1^2] \\
     &= S_{XX} \left( \text{Var}(\hat\beta_1) + (E[\hat\beta_1])^2 \right) \\
     &= S_{XX} \left( \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{XX}} + \beta_1^2 \right) \\
     &= \sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{XX}.
\end{align*}\]

And \(E[MSR] = E[SSR/1] = \sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{XX}\).


7.0.8 Expected Mean Squares

It can be shown that \[E(MSE) = \sigma^2.\]
When \(\beta_1=0\), \(E(MSR) = E(MSE) = \sigma^2\).
When \(\beta_1 \neq 0\), \(E(MSR) > E(MSE)\).
This justifies the F-test for testing \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) vs. \(H_a: \beta_1 \neq 0\).



7.0.9 F Test

For testing \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) vs. \(H_a: \beta_1 \neq 0\), the F-statistic is \[F = \frac{MSR}{MSE}.\]
We reject \(H_0\) if \(F\) is too large

The rejection region is \(F > F_{\alpha, 1, n-2}\), where \(F_{\alpha, 1, n-2}\) is the \((1-\alpha)\) quantile of the \(F\) distribution with 1 and \(n-2\) degrees of freedom.

The p-value is \(P(F_{1, n-2} \geq F_{\text{obs}})\), where \(F_{\text{obs}}\) is the observed value of the F-statistic.



7.0.10 F test and t-test

The F-statistic can be rewritten as \[F = \frac{MSR}{MSE} = \frac{\hat\beta_1^2 S_{XX}}{s^2} = \left( \frac{\hat\beta_1}{s/\sqrt{S_{XX}}} \right)^2 = t^2,\] where \(t = \hat\beta_1 / (s/\sqrt{S_{XX}})\) is the t-statistic for testing \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\).
Thus, the F-test and the t-test for testing \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) are equivalent in SLR.
In fact, as \(F_{1,n-2}\) distribution is also equivalent to the distribution of the square of a random variable whose distribution is \(t_{n-2}\), the F test is equivalent to the two-sided t test.

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
2.1 Simple Linear Regression

In a Simple Linear Regression Model, a single predictor (independent/explanatory variable) is used to predict a response/dependent variable

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
2.2 Simple Linear Regression

A simple linear regression line describes a linear relationship between __ and __: \[E(y|x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\]
The simple linear regression model \[y=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \epsilon\] where \(\epsilon\) is random error.

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
2.3 Notation

For the individual \(i\): \[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i, \quad i=1, \cdots, n\]
\(\beta_0, \beta_1\): regression coefficients (uknown parameters)

\(\beta_0\): intercept
\(\beta_1\): slop

\(y_i\): observed response value of individual \(i\)
\(x_i\): observed predictor value of individual \(i\)
\(\epsilon_i\): random error of individual \(i\)

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
2.4 Assumptions: Basic (a)

Basic assumptions

Linearity: The relationship between the predictor and the mean of the response is linear. \[E(y_i|x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\] Equivalently, \[E(\epsilon)=0\]
Uncorrelated errors: The errors are uncorrelated. \[Cov(\epsilon_i, \epsilon_j)=0, \quad i\neq j\]
Homoscedasticity: The errors have constant variance at all levels of the predictor. \[Var(\epsilon_i)=\sigma^2, i=1, \cdots, n\]

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
2.5 Assumptions: Stronger (b)

Stronger assumptions

Linearity
Independence: The errors are independent.
Homoscedasticity
Normality: The errors are normally distributed.

The above assumptions are equivalent to \[\epsilon_1, \cdots, \epsilon_n \overset{iid} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\]

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
2.6 Implications of Assumptions (a)
Regression Model: \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i, \quad i=1, \cdots, n\)

For a given \(x_i\), under the basic assumptions (a) or (b), we have

\(y_i\) is a random variable
\(E(y_i|x_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\)
\(Var(y_i|x_i) = \sigma^2\)
\(Cov(y_i, y_j|x_i, x_j)=0, i\neq j\),

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
2.7 Implications of Assumptions (b)
Regression Model: \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i, \quad i=1, \cdots, n\)

For a given \(x_i\), under the assumptions (b), we have

\(y_i \sim N(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i, \sigma^2)\)
\(y_1, \cdots, y_n\) are independent

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
3.1 Estimate coefficients

Predicted / Fitted values \(\hat{y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i\).
Observed errors (residuals) \(e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i = y_i - \hat{\beta}_0 - \hat{\beta}_1 x_i\).
Sum of Squared Errors (SSE), also known as Residual Sum of Squares (RSS): \[RSS = SSE= \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2=\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \hat\beta_1 x_i)^2\]
The Least Squares Estimation (LSE) criterion chooses \(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1\) that minimizes RSS (SSE).

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
3.2 Normal Equations

The normal equations are obtained by setting the partial derivatives of RSS with respect to \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\) to zero: \[\frac{\partial RSS}{\partial \hat{\beta}_0} = -2 \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{\beta}_0 - \hat{\beta}_1 x_i) = 0\] \[\frac{\partial RSS}{\partial \hat{\beta}_1} = -2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i (y_i - \hat{\beta}_0 - \hat{\beta}_1 x_i) = 0\]
Solving these equations gives the least squares estimates.

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
3.3 Least Squares Estimates

The least squares estimates for the coefficients are: \[\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}\] \[\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}\] where \(\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\) and \(\bar{y} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n y_i\) are the sample means of \(x\) and \(y\), respectively.

\(\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1\) are called least squares estimators.

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
section: 3.4 Sum of Squares in Simple Linear Regression
text:
3.4 Sum of Squares in Simple Linear Regression

\(S_{yy}=\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2\), total sum of Squares of \(y\)
\(S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2\), total sum of Squares of \(x\)
\(S_{xy}=\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})\), covariance sum of Squares.

The least squares estimates can be expressed as: \[\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}, \quad \hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}\] It can be shown that \(SSE=S_{yy} - \hat\beta_1 S_{xy} = S_{yy} - \frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}}\).

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
section: 3.5 Properties of Fitted Values and Residuals
text:
3.5 Properties of Fitted Values and Residuals

The sum of the residuals is zero: \(\sum_{i=1}^n e_i = 0\).
The least squares regression line passes through the point \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\) because \(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \bar x = \bar y\) (by the normal equation).
The sum of the observed values = the sum of the fitted values: \[\sum_{i=1}^n y_i = \sum_{i=1}^n \hat{y}_i\]
The sum of the residuals weighted by the predictor values or predicted values is zero: \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i e_i = 0, \sum_{i=1}^n \hat{y}_i e_i  = 0\]

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
4.1 Estimate \(\sigma^2\)

An intuitive estimate of \(\sigma^2\) might be: \[s^2 = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 = \frac{SSE}{n}\]
However, this estimate is biased because the residuals \(e_i\) are not independent and have less variability than the true errors \(\epsilon_i\).
An unbiased estimate of \(\sigma^2\) is: \[s^2 = \frac{1}{n-2} \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 = \frac{SSE}{n-2}=MSE\]

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
5.1 Sum of Squares Decomposition

Total Sum of Squares (SST): \[SST = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2\]
Regression Sum of Squares (SSR): \[SSR = \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2\] The variation explained by the predictor (regression model).
Error Sum of Squares (SSE): \[SSE = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\]

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
5.2 Sums of Squares

It can be shown that: \[SST = SSR + SSE\]

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
5.3 Coefficient of Determination \(R^2\)

The coefficient of determination \(R^2\) is defined as: \[R^2 = \frac{SSR}{SST} = 1 - \frac{SSE}{SST}\]
\(R^2\) represents the proportion of variance in the response variable that is explained by the predictor variable.

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
5.4 Correlation

The correlation coefficient, \(\rho\), provides a measure of the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables, \(x\) and \(y\).
The sample correlation coefficient \(r\) between \(x\) and \(y\) is given by: \[r = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar x)(y_i -\bar y)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)^2 \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar y)^2}} =\frac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} S_{yy}}}\]
It can be shown that in simple linear regression, the coefficient of determination \(R^2\) is equal to the square of the sample correlation coefficient \(r\):

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
5.5 Summary

LSE of \(\beta_0, \beta_1\): \[\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}, \quad \hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}\]
Variance estimate: \[s^2 = \frac{SSE}{n-2}= \frac{1}{n-2} (S_{yy}- \frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}})\]
Coefficient of determination: \[R^2 = \frac{SSR}{SST} = \frac{SST-SSE}{SST} = \frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx} S_{yy}} = r^2\]

title: Lec 01: Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
5.6 Useful Formulas

Useful formulas for calculating \(S_{XX}, S_{YY}, S_{XY}\): \[\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar x)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 - n \bar x^2\] \[\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar y)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2 - n \bar y^2\] \[\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y) = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - n \bar x \bar y\]
Sufficient statistics for conducting regression analysis : \(n, \sum x_i, \sum y_i, \sum x_i^2, \sum y_i^2, \sum x_i y_i\)

text:
6.6 How to Calculate Simple Linear Regression Estimates
Given summary statistics
- \(n = 41\)
- \(\sum x_i = -149.953,\; \sum y_i = 115.0934\)
- \(\sum x_i^2 = 554.024,\; \sum y_i^2 = 324.0225\)
- \(\sum x_i y_i = -423.0244\)

Step 1. Compute sufficient statistics
\[
\bar{x} = \tfrac{-149.953}{41} \approx -3.66,
\quad
\bar{y} = \tfrac{115.0934}{41} \approx 2.81
\]
\[
S_{xx} = 554.024 - \tfrac{(-149.953)^2}{41} \approx 5.59
\]
\[
S_{yy} = 324.0225 - \tfrac{(115.0934)^2}{41} \approx 0.94
\]
\[
S_{xy} = -423.0244 - \tfrac{(-149.953)(115.0934)}{41} \approx -2.08
\]

Step 2. Regression coefficients
\[
\hat\beta_1 = \tfrac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}} \approx \tfrac{-2.08}{5.59} \approx -0.37
\]
\[
\hat\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \hat\beta_1 \bar{x}
   \approx 2.81 - (-0.37)(-3.66)
   \approx 1.46
\]

Step 3. Error variance
\[
\hat\sigma^2 = \tfrac{1}{n-2}\left(S_{yy} - \hat\beta_1 S_{xy}\right)
= \tfrac{1}{39}(0.94 - (-0.37)(-2.08))
\approx \tfrac{0.17}{39}
\]
\[
\hat\sigma \approx  \sqrt{\ 0.0044} \approx 0.066;
\]

\(\hat\beta_0 \approx 1.46\):

\(R^2 = \frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx} S_{yy}} \approx \frac{(-2.08)^2}{5.59 \times 0.94} \approx 0.82\)
About 82% of the variability in log10(cycleLife) can be explained by the linear relationship with log10(DeltaQvar).
\(r = \frac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} S_{yy}}} \approx \frac{-2.08}{\sqrt{5.59 \times 0.94}} \approx -0.91\).

text:
2.1 What is Statistical Inference

Broadly speaking, statistical inference is the process of drawing conclusions about a population based on a sample of data from that population.
There are different types of statistical inference, including:

Estimation: Estimating population parameters (e.g., mean, variance) based on sample statistics.
Hypothesis Testing: Testing assumptions or claims about population parameters using sample data.
Prediction: Making predictions about future observations based on a fitted model.

So far, we have learned how to estimate \(\beta_0, \beta_1\) and \(\sigma^2\) in SLR. Next, we will learn how to do inference in SLR.

title: Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
section: 2.3 How did we do inference for one-sample problems?
text:
2.3 How did we do inference for one-sample problems?

To understand inference in SLR, let’s first review how we did inference for one-sample problems.
A random sample \(y_1, y_2, \cdots, y_n \overset{iid}\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\).
The parameter of interest: \(\mu\) (unknown).
Point estimate of \(\mu\). \(\bar{y}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\) to estimate the population mean \(\mu\).
Sampling distribution of \(\bar{y}\): \(\bar{y} \sim N(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{n})\).
But \(\sigma^2\) is unknown. We estimate it by \(s^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\bar{y})^2\).
Standard error (SE) of \(\bar{y}\): \(SE(\bar{y}) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\).

title: Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
text:
2.4 Inference: hypothesis testing

Hypothesis test: \(H_0: \mu=\mu_0\) vs \(H_a: \mu\neq \mu_0\).
Test statistic: \[t=\frac{\bar{y}-\mu_0}{SE(\bar{y})}=\frac{\bar{y}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}} \overset{H_0}\sim t_{n-1}\]
Not normal? \(y_1, y_2, \cdots, y_n \overset{iid}\sim (\mu, \sigma^2)\). The results can still be used when \(n\) is large enough. Why?

title: Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
text:
2.5 Inference Confidence Interval

A 100(1-\(\alpha\))% confidence interval for \(\mu\) is given by: \[\bar{y} \pm t_{\alpha/2, n-1} \times SE(\bar{y}) = \bar{y} \pm t_{\alpha/2, n-1} \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
The standard error (SE) quantifies the precision of the estimate. The smaller the SE, the more precise the estimate.
The critical value \(t_{\alpha/2, n-1}\) determines the width of the confidence interval. A larger critical value (smaller \(\alpha\)) results in a wider interval.

section: 3.2 Review: Properties of Expectation and Variance
text:
3.2 Review: Properties of Expectation and Variance
A random variable \(X\sim (\mu, \sigma^2)\), i.e., \(E(X)=\mu, Var(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2]=\sigma^2\)

\(E(aX+b)=aE(X)+b=a\mu+b\)
\(Var(aX+b)=a^2 Var(X)=a^2 \sigma^2\)

For random variables \(X_1, X_2\),

\(E(X_1+X_2)=E(X_1)+E(X_2)\)
If \(X_1, X_2\) are independent, then \(Var(X_1+X_2)=Var(X_1)+Var(X_2)\).

Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
text:
3.5 Variance of \(\hat\beta_1\)

Recall that \(Var(y_i)=Var(\epsilon_i)=\sigma^2\) and \(y_i's\) are uncorrelated (a stronger assumption is independence)


\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1)
&= \operatorname{Var}\!\left[
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar{x})y_i}{S_{xx}}
\right] \\[6pt]
&= \frac{1}{S_{xx}^2}\,
   \operatorname{Var}\!\left[
   \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar{x})y_i
   \right] \\[6pt]
&= \frac{1}{S_{xx}^2}
   \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar{x})^2\,
   \operatorname{Var}(y_i) \\[6pt]
&= \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}^2}
   \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar{x})^2 \\[6pt]
&= \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
text:
4.1 Distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\) when \(\sigma^2\) is known

Since \(\hat\beta_1\) is a linear combination of \(y_i's\) and \(y_i's\) are normally distributed, \(\hat\beta_1\) is also normally distributed.
Thus, when \(\sigma^2\) is known, we have \[\hat\beta_1 \sim N(\beta_1, \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}})\]
The standardized version: \[Z=\frac{\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1}{\sqrt{Var(\hat\beta_1)}} = \frac{\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1}{\sqrt{\sigma^2/S_{xx}}}=\frac{\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}} \sim N(0, 1)\]

title: Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
text:
4.2 CI for \(\beta_1\) when \(\sigma^2\) is known

Because \(\frac{\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}  \sim N(0, 1)\), we have

\[P\left(-z_{1-\alpha/2} \leq \frac{\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}} \leq z_{1-\alpha/2}\right) = 1-\alpha\] Therefore, a 100(1-\(\alpha\))% confidence interval for \(\beta_1\) is given by: \[(\hat\beta_1 - z_{1-\alpha/2} \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}, \hat\beta_1 + z_{1-\alpha/2} \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}})\] Note \(-z_{1-\alpha/2} = z_{\alpha/2}\).

title: Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
text:
4.3 Distribution of \(\hat\beta_1\) when \(\sigma^2\) is unknown

When \(\sigma^2\) is unknown, we estimate it by \(s^2=\frac{SSE}{n-2}\).
We define \(\hat{Var}(\hat{\beta_1})=\frac{s^2}{S_{xx}}\) and the estimated standard error \(SE(\hat\beta_1)=\sqrt{\hat{Var}(\hat{\beta_1})}=\frac{s}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\).
The standardized version: \[\frac{\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1}{SE(\hat\beta_1)} = \frac{\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1}{s/\sqrt{S_{xx}}} \]

title: Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
section: 4.4 How to construct a t-distributed statistic?
text:
4.4 How to construct a t-distributed statistic?

Let \(Z\) be a standard normal random variable
Let \(U\) be a chi-square random variable with \(v\) degrees of freedom
Suppose \(Z\) and \(U\) are independent
Then the random variable \[T=\frac{Z}{\sqrt{U/v}}\] has a t-distribution with \(v\) degrees of freedom, i.e., \(T\sim t_v\).

title: Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
section: 4.5 Details about the t-statistic in SLR
text:
4.5 Details about the t-statistic in SLR
The assumptions of the SLR model: 1. \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i, \quad \text{where } \epsilon_1, \cdots, \epsilon_n \overset{iid}\sim N(0, \sigma^2)\)
Under the assumptions, we can show

\(\hat\beta_1 \sim N(\beta_1, \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}})\), which implies that \[Z=\frac{\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}} \sim N(0, 1)\]
\(\hat\beta_1\) and \(s^2\) are independent, which implies that \(Z\) and \(s^2\) are independent.
\(\frac{(n-2)s^2}{\sigma^2}=\frac{SSE}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-2}\).

title: Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
section: 4.6 Details about the t-statistic in SLR
text:
4.6 Details about the t-statistic in SLR

By the way to construct a t-distributed statistic, we have \[T=\frac{Z}{\sqrt{U/(n-2)}}\sim t_{n-2}\] where \(Z=\frac{\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1}{\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\) and \(U=\frac{(n-2)s^2}{\sigma^2}\).

Thus, we have \[T=\frac{\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1}{s/\sqrt{S_{xx}}} =\frac{\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1}{SE(\hat\beta_1)}  \sim t_{n-2}\]

Note that we have \(n-2\) degrees of freedom because we estimated two parameters \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) in SLR.

title: Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
text:
5.1 CI for \(\beta_1\) when \(\sigma^2\) is unknown

Because \(\frac{\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1}{SE(\hat\beta_1)} \sim t_{n-2}\), we have

\[P\left(-t_{n-2, 1-\alpha/2} \leq \frac{\hat\beta_1 - \beta_1}{SE(\hat\beta_1)} \leq t_{n-2, 1-\alpha/2}\right) = 1-\alpha\]

Therefore, a 100(1-\(\alpha\))% confidence interval for \(\beta_1\) is given by: \[(\hat\beta_1 - t_{n-2, 1-\alpha/2} SE(\hat\beta_1), \hat\beta_1 + t_{n-2, 1-\alpha/2} SE(\hat\beta_1))\] where \(SE(\hat\beta_1)=\frac{s}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\).

title: Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
text:
6.1 Hypothesis Testing in SLR

We will focus on hypothesis testing for \(\beta_1\).
In SLR, we are often interested in testing whether there is a linear relationship between \(x\) and \(y\).
The null hypothesis is that there is no linear relationship, i.e., \(\beta_1=0\).
The alternative hypothesis is that there is a linear relationship, i.e., \(\beta_1 \neq 0\).
Thus, we want to test the following hypotheses: \[H_0: \beta_1=0 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \beta_1 \neq 0\]

title: Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
section: 6.2 Hypothesis testing in general: Five steps
text:
6.2 Hypothesis testing in general: Five steps

Step 1: State the null and alternative hypotheses.
Step 2: Choose a significance level \(\alpha\).
Step 3: Calculate a test statistic using the sample.
Step 4: Determine the rejection region or p-value.
Step 5: Make a decision and interpret the results.

title: Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
text:
6.3 Test Statistic for \(\beta_1\)

The test statistic is given by: \[T=\frac{\hat\beta_1 - 0}{SE(\hat\beta_1)} = \frac{\hat\beta_1}{s/\sqrt{S_{xx}}}\]
When \(H_0\) is true, i.e., \(\beta_1=0\), \(T \sim t_{n-2}\).

title: Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
text:
6.4 Rejection/critical Region and p-value

Rejection region approach: Reject \(H_0\) if \(|T| > t_{n-2, 1-\alpha/2}\).
p-value approach: The p-value (two-sided) is given by \[p-value = 2P(T \geq |t_{obs}|)\] where \(t_{obs}\) is the observed value of the test statistic \(T\). What is the distribution of \(T\)?

If \(p-value < \alpha\), we reject \(H_0\).
If \(p-value \geq \alpha\), we fail to reject \(H_0\). (there is not enough evidence to reject \(H_0\)).

6.8 One-sided tests: \(H_1: \beta_1 > 0\)

We can also perform one-sided tests. For example, to test \[H_0: \beta_1 \leq 0 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \beta_1 > 0\]

Rejection region approach: Reject \(H_0\) if \(T > t_{n-2, 1-\alpha}\).
p-value approach: The p-value (right-sided) is given by \[p-value = P(T \geq t_{obs})\] We reject \(H_0\) if \(p-value < \alpha\).

title: Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
text:
6.9 One-sided tests: \(H_1: \beta_1 > 0\)

In some applications, we may be interested in testing one-sided alternatives. For example, we would like to know whether Mount Airy has a positive linear relationship with Charleston, i.e.,
\[H_0: \beta_1 \geq 0 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \beta_1 < 0\]

Rejection region approach: Reject \(H_0\) if \(T < -t_{n-2, 1-\alpha}\).
p-value approach: The p-value (left-sided) is given by \[p-value = P(T \leq t_{obs})\]

title: Lec 02: Inference In Simple Linear Regression
text:
6.10 Example: Mount Airy and Charleston

For the Mount Airy and Charleston example, we have \(t_{obs} = 3.24\) and \(n-2=83\).
The critical value \(t_{83, 0.95} \approx 1.66\). We reject the null hypothesis because \(3.24 > 1.66\).
The p-value is given by \(P(T \geq 3.24) \approx 0.00085\) (using R). We reject the null hypothesis because \(0.00085 < 0.05\).

Total Sum of Squares (SST): \[SST = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2\]

2.3 Decomposition of the Total Sum of Squares
It can be shown that: \[SST = SSR + SSE\]
Proof: \[\begin{align*}
SST &= \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2 \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^n \big[(y_i - \hat{y}_i) + (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})\big]^2 \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2 + 2\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y}) \\
    &= SSE + SSR + 2\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})
\end{align*}\] 
The last term is zero because

Don’t remember the normal equations? Here is the derivation \[\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2 &= -2 \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i) = 0, \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_1} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2 &= -2 \sum_{i=1}^n X_i (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i) = 0.
\end{align*}\] 
The above two equations are called the normal equations. They can be rewritten as \[\sum_{i=1}^n e_i = 0 \quad\text{and}\quad \sum_{i=1}^n e_i X_i = 0.\]

title: Lec 04: ANOVA and Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
3.1 ANOVA Table for SLR

An analysis of variance (ANOVA) table summarizes the results of the regression analysis. It typically has 5 or 6 columns.

Source of variation (Regression, Error, Total)
Degrees of freedom (DF)
Sum of squares (SS)
Mean square (MS = SS/DF)
F-statistic (for testing \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) vs. \(H_a: \beta_1 \neq 0\))
p-value (optional)

title: Lec 04: ANOVA and Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
3.2 ANOVA Table for SLR
\[\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\textbf{Source} & \textbf{DF} & \textbf{SS} & \textbf{MS} & \textbf{F} \\
\hline
Regression & 1 & SSR & MSR = SSR/1 & F = MSR/MSE \\
Error      & n-2 & SSE & MSE = SSE/(n-2) & \\
Total      & n-1 & SST & & \\
\hline
\end{array}\]

DF: degrees of freedom
SS: sum of squares
MS: mean square (SS divided by corresponding DF)
F: F-statistic for testing \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) vs. \(H_a: \beta_1 \neq 0\)
Under \(H_0\), \(F \sim F_{1, n-2}\).
\(R^2\) can be computed from the table. (how?)

title: Lec 04: ANOVA and Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
3.3 E[SSR]

We will rewrite SSR in terms of \(\hat\beta_1\):

\[\begin{align*}
SSR &= \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2 \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 X_i - \bar{y})^2 \\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat\beta_1 (X_i - \bar{X}))^2 \quad\text{(since $\hat\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \hat\beta_1 \bar{X}$)}\\
    &= \hat\beta_1^2 \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2 = \hat\beta_1^2 S_{XX}.
\end{align*}\] - Therefore, \[E[SSR]=E[\hat\beta_1^2]S_{XX}.\]

title: Lec 04: ANOVA and Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
3.4 E[MSR]

We find that \(SSR=\hat\beta_1^2 S_{XX}\). But \(\hat\beta_1 \sim N(\beta_1, \sigma^2/S_{XX})\). Note that \(Var(\hat\beta_1) = E(\hat\beta_1^2) - E^2[\hat\beta_1]\). Therefore, \[\begin{align*}
E[SSR] &= E[\hat\beta_1^2 S_{XX}] \\
     &= S_{XX} E[\hat\beta_1^2] \\
     &= S_{XX} \left( \text{Var}(\hat\beta_1) + (E[\hat\beta_1])^2 \right) \\
     &= S_{XX} \left( \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{XX}} + \beta_1^2 \right) \\
     &= \sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{XX}.
\end{align*}\]

Note that \(MSR = SSR/1 = \hat\beta_1^2 S_{XX},\) and \(E[MSR] = E[SSR/1] = \sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{XX}\).

title: Lec 04: ANOVA and Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
3.5 E[SSE]
\[\begin{align*}
E[SSE] &= E\left[\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\right] = E\left[\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2\right] = E[e'e] \\
       &= E[(Y - \hat{Y})'(Y - \hat{Y})] = E[Y'(I - H)'(I - H)Y] \\
       &= E[Y'(I - H)Y] \quad\text{(since $I-H$ is symmetric and idempotent)} \\
       &= E[\text{trace}((I - H)YY')] \quad\text{(since trace is invariant under cyclic permutations)} \\
       &= \text{trace}((I - H)E[YY']) \\
       &= \text{trace}((I - H)(Var(Y) + E[Y]E[Y]')) \\
       &= \text{trace}((I - H)(\sigma^2 I + X\beta\beta'X')) \\
       &= \sigma^2 \text{trace}(I - H) + \text{trace}((I - H)X\beta\beta'X') \\
       &= \sigma^2 (n - 2) + 0 \quad\text{(since $(I-H)X = 0$)} \\
       &= (n-2)\sigma^2.
\end{align*}\]

title: Lec 04: ANOVA and Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
3.6 E[MSE]

Because \(MSE=SSE/(n-2)\), we have \[E(MSE) = \sigma^2.\]
When \(\beta_1=0\), \(E(MSR) = E(MSE) = \sigma^2\).
When \(\beta_1 \neq 0\), \(E(MSR) > E(MSE)\).
This justifies the F-test for testing \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) vs. \(H_a: \beta_1 \neq 0\).

title: Lec 04: ANOVA and Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
4.1 Construct F Test Statistics

F-distributed statistics can be constructed as the ratio of two independent chi-square distributed statistics divided by their degrees of freedom. Let

\(U \sim \chi^2_{d_1}\)
\(V \sim \chi^2_{d_2}\)
\(U\) and \(V\) are independent.

Then \[F = \frac{U/d_1}{V/d_2} \sim F_{d_1, d_2}.\]

title: Lec 04: ANOVA and Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
4.2 F-test in SLR

In SLR, we can show that

\(SSE/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-2}\)
\(SSR/\sigma^2 \overset{\textcolor{red}{when?}}\sim \chi^2_1\)
\(SSR\) and \(SSE\) are independent.

Therefore, \[F = \frac{MSR}{MSE} = \frac{SSR/1}{SSE/(n-2)}  \overset{\textcolor{red}{when?}} \sim F_{1, n-2}.\]

title: Lec 04: ANOVA and Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
4.3 F Test

It turns out that

\[SSR/\sigma^2 \overset{\textcolor{red}{H_0: \beta_1=0}}\sim \chi^2_1\]

Also, we have shown that \[E[MSR] = \sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{XX}, E[MSE]=\sigma^2\]
Both suggest that we should reject \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) when the ratio \(F = MSR/MSE\) is too large.
We reject \(H_0\) if \(F\) is too large: the rejection region is \(F > F_{\alpha, 1, n-2}\), where \(F_{\alpha, 1, n-2}\) is the \((1-\alpha)\) quantile of the \(F_{1, n-2}\) distribution.
The p-value is \(P(F_{1, n-2} \geq F_{\text{obs}})\), where \(F_{\text{obs}}\) is the observed value of the F-statistic.

text:
4.6 F test and t-test

The F-statistic can be rewritten as \[F = \frac{MSR}{MSE} = \frac{\hat\beta_1^2 S_{XX}}{s^2} = \left( \frac{\hat\beta_1}{s/\sqrt{S_{XX}}} \right)^2 = t^2,\] where \(t = \hat\beta_1 / (s/\sqrt{S_{XX}})\) is the t-statistic for testing \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\).
Thus, the F-test and the t-test for testing \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) are equivalent in SLR.
In fact, as \(F_{1,n-2}\) distribution is also equivalent to the distribution of the square of a random variable whose distribution is \(t_{n-2}\), the F test is equivalent to the two-sided t test.

title: Lec 04: ANOVA and Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
5.1 Compare Two Nested Models

F tests can be used to compared nested models

Here, nested models mean that one model (the reduced model) is a special case of the other model (the full model) with some parameters set to zero.

For Simple Linear Regression (SLR), the two following models are nested:

Reduced model: \(y_i = \beta_0 + \epsilon_i\), \(\rightarrow SSE_R\), note \(SSE_R=SST\).
Full model: \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i}+ \epsilon_i\), \(\rightarrow SSE_F\), note \(SSE_F=SSE\).

The reduced model is obtained from the full model by setting \(\beta_1 = 0\).
The difference in SEE between the two models is due to the inclusion of the predictor variable \(x\) in the full model: \(SSE_R - SSE_F = SST - SSE = SSR\).

title: Lec 04: ANOVA and Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
5.2 Compare Two Nested Models

Let \(SSE_F\) and \(SSE_R\) be the SSE for the full and reduced models, respectively.
Note that \(SSE_F \leq SSE_R\) because the full model has more parameters and thus fits the data at least as well as the reduced model.
We can construct the following F-statistic to compare the two models: \[F = \frac{(SSE_R - SSE_F)/(df_R - df_F)}{SSE_F/df_F}\] where \(df_F=n-2\) and \(df_R=n-1\) are the degrees of freedom for the full and reduced models, respectively.
Under \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\), \(F \sim F_{df_F - df_R, df_F}\).

title: Lec 04: ANOVA and Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
6.1 F test and \(R^2\)

The coefficient of determination, \(R^2\), is defined as \[R^2 = \frac{SSR}{SST} = 1 - \frac{SSE}{SST}.\]
\(R^2\) measures the proportion of the variance in the response variable that is explained by the predictor variable.
\(R^2\) is always between 0 and 1. A value of 0 indicates that the model does not explain any of the variance in the response variable, while a value of 1 indicates that the model explains all of the variance.

title: Lec 04: ANOVA and Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
6.2 F test and \(R^2\)

The F-statistic can be rewritten in terms of \(R^2\) as follows: \[\begin{align*}
F &= \frac{MSR}{MSE} = \frac{SSR/1}{SSE/(n-2)} \\
  &= \frac{(R^2 \cdot SST)/1}{((1 - R^2) \cdot SST)/(n-2)} \\
  &= \frac{R^2}{1 - R^2} \cdot (n - 2).
\end{align*}\]
Therefore, the F-test for testing \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) vs. \(H_a: \beta_1 \neq 0\) is equivalent to testing whether \(R^2\) is significantly greater than 0.

title: Lec 04: ANOVA and Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
6.3 F test and \(R^2\)

The p-value for the F-test can be computed as \[\text{p-value} = P(F_{1, n-2} \geq F_{\text{obs}}) = P\left(F_{1, n-2} \geq \frac{R^2}{1 - R^2} \cdot (n - 2)\right).\]
Because of the relationship between and \(F\) and \(R^2\), under \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\), we have \[\frac{R^2}{1 - R^2} \cdot (n - 2) \overset{H_0: \beta_1=0} \sim F_{1, n-2}.\]
Is there a name of the null distribution of \(R^2\)?

title: Lec 04: ANOVA and Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
6.4 F test and \(R^2\)

Yes, its called the Beta distribution. Specifically, under \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\), \[R^2 \overset{H_0: \beta_1=0}\sim \text{Beta}\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{n-2}{2}\right).\]
In fact, there is a connection between F and Beta distributions:

If \(F \sim F_{d_1, d_2}\), then \(\frac{d_1 F}{d_1 F + d_2} \sim \text{Beta}\left(\frac{d_1}{2}, \frac{d_2}{2}\right)\).
Conversely, if \(B \sim \text{Beta}\left(\frac{d_1}{2}, \frac{d_2}{2}\right)\), then \(\frac{d_2 B}{d_1 (1 - B)} \sim F_{d_1, d_2}\).

title: Lec 04: ANOVA and Diagnostics In Simple Linear Regression
text:
6.5 Correlation Coeficient

The correlation coefficient, \(r\), between the response variable \(y\) and the predictor variable \(x\) is defined as \[r = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2}}.\]
We have shown the relationship between \(\hat\beta_1\) and \(r\): \[\hat\beta_1 = r \frac{S_Y}{S_X},\] where \(S_Y\) and \(S_X\) are the sample standard deviations of \(y\) and \(x\), respectively.
It can be shown that: \[t = r \sqrt{\frac{n-2}{1-r^2}} \text{, which has been shown} \overset{H_0: \beta_1=0}\sim t_{n-2}.\]

section: 2.1 Lack of Fit Test in SLR
text:
2.1 Lack of Fit Test in SLR

We have introduced visualization methods to check the linear model assumptions.
Goodness-of-fit tests (GOF) are often used to assess whether a statistical model/distribution fits the data well.

For example, the Chi-square goodness-of-fit test is used to test whether observed categorical data follow a specified distribution.
For simple linear regression, we consider the lack for fit test (LOF), which is an F-test, to test whether the linear regression model is a good fit for the data.

title: Lec 06: Lack of Fit Test and Data Transformation
section: 2.2 Lack of Fit Test in SLR: Notations
text:
2.2 Lack of Fit Test in SLR: Notations

LOF test requires replicated \(x\) values (i.e., multiple \(y\) values for the same \(x\) value).
\(k\): the number of unique \(x\) values
\(n_i\): the number of replicates for the \(i\)th unique \(x\) value
\(n = \sum_{i=1}^k n_i\): the total number of observations.
\(y_{ij}\): the \(j\)th observation of the response variable \(y\) at the \(i\)th unique value of the predictor variable \(x\), where \(i = 1, 2, \ldots, k\) and \(j = 1, 2, \ldots, n_i\).



Code
set.seed(123)
x <- rep(1:5, each=3)
y <- x^2 + rnorm(15, 0, 1) # true model is quadratic
data <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)
# Reduced model: y_i = beta_0 + beta_1 x_i + epsilon_i
fit_reduced <- lm(y ~ x, data = data)
# Full model: y_i = mu_i + epsilon_i
fit_full <- lm(y ~ factor(x), data = data)
plot(data$x, data$y, pch=19, xlab="x", ylab="y", main="Lack of Fit Test Example 2")

section: 2.3 Lack of Fit Test in SLR
text:
2.3 Lack of Fit Test in SLR
A LOF test compares two models:

Reduced model \(H_0\): \(y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_{ij}\); assumes a linear relationship between \(x\) and \(y\).
Full model \(H_1\): \(y_{ij} = \mu_i + \epsilon_{ij}\), where \(\mu_i\) is the mean of the \(y\) values for the \(i\)th unique \(x\) value; uses a separate mean for each unique \(x\) value.

title: Lec 06: Lack of Fit Test and Data Transformation
section: 2.4 Lack of Fit Test in SLR: Sum of Squares
text:
2.4 Lack of Fit Test in SLR: Sum of Squares

The reduced model (\(H_0\)), which is the SLR: \[SSE_R = \sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (y_{ij} - \hat{y}_{ij})=(y_{ij}-\hat{\beta}_0 - \hat{\beta}_1 x_i)^2\] where \(\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1\) are the LSE of the SLR, and \(SSE_R\) is the SEE of the SLR.
The full model (\(H_1)\)): \[SSE_F = \sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (y_{ij} - \bar{y}_i)^2\] where \(\bar{y}_i\) is the mean of the \(y\) values for the \(i\)th unique \(x\) value.
Which one is smaller? Why?

title: Lec 06: Lack of Fit Test and Data Transformation
section: 2.5 Lack of Fit Test in SLR: F-test
text:
2.5 Lack of Fit Test in SLR: F-test

The full model has more parameters and thus fits the data at least as well as the reduced model. As a result, \(SSE_F \leq SSE_R\).
We can construct the following F-statistic to compare the SSEs: \[F = \frac{(SSE_R - SSE_F)/(df_R - df_F)}{SSE_F/df_F}\] where \(df_F\) and \(df_R\) are the degrees of freedom for the full and reduced models, respectively.
Under \(H_0\): the linear model fits the data well, \(F \sim F_{df_R - df_F, df_F}\).
What are \(df_F\) and \(df_R\)?

title: Lec 06: Lack of Fit Test and Data Transformation
section: 2.6 Lack of Fit Test in SLR: Decomposition of SSE
text:
2.6 Lack of Fit Test in SLR: Decomposition of SSE

\(SSE_R\) can be decomposed \[\begin{align*}
SSE_R &= \sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (y_{ij} - \hat{y}_{ij})^2 = \sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (y_{ij} - \bar{y}_i + \bar{y}_i - \hat{y}_{ij})^2 \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (y_{ij} - \bar{y}_i)^2 + \sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (\bar{y}_i - \hat{y}_{ij})^2 + 2\sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (y_{ij} - \bar{y}_i)(\bar{y}_i - \hat{y}_{ij}) \\
&= SSE_F + SS_{LF} + 0 \\
&= SSE_F + SS_{LF}
\end{align*}\]
where \(SS_{LOF} = \sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (\bar{y}_i - \hat{y}_{ij})^2\) is the sum of squares due to lack of fit.

title: Lec 06: Lack of Fit Test and Data Transformation
section: 2.7 Lack of Fit Test in SLR: degrees of freedom
text:
2.7 Lack of Fit Test in SLR: degrees of freedom

We need to find the degrees of freedom for the full and reduced models.
For the full model, we estimate \(k\) means (\(\mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots, \mu_k\)) from \(n\) observations. Thus, \(df_F = n - k\).
For the reduced model, we estimate 2 parameters (\(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\)) from \(n\) observations. Thus, \(df_R = n - 2\).
Therefore, the F-statistic can be rewritten as \[F = \frac{(SSE_R - SSE_F)/(k - 2)}{SSE_F/(n - k)} = \frac{SS_{LOF}/(k - 2)}{SSE_F/(n - k)}\]
Under \(H_0\): the linear model fits the data well, \(F \sim F_{k - 2, n - k}\).

section: 2.18 When Assume Model Is not Reasonable/Adequate
text:
2.18 When Assume Model Is not Reasonable/Adequate

When one or several assumptions of the linear model are violated, what can we do?
Consider more complex models. For example,

If the relationship between \(x\) and \(y\) is not linear, we may consider polynomial regression or other types of regression (e.g., spline regression, generalized additive models).
If the variance of the errors is not constant, we may consider weighted least squares or generalized least squares.

We may consider data transformation.

Next, we present how to transform the data to address non-linearity or non-constant variance.

title: Lec 06: Lack of Fit Test and Data Transformation
text:
3.1 Data Transformation: General Rules

Transformations are often used to achieve linearity, constant variance, and normality of errors.
Transform \(x\) or \(y\)?
Not linear: If the relationship between \(x\) and \(y\) is not linear but residuals are generally normal and have constant variance, we may consider transforming \(x\).
Not constant variance: If the variance of \(y\) varies with \(x\), consider transforming \(y\) (e.g., log or square root).
If both the relationship and the variance are problematic, we may consider transforming \(y\) to stabilize variance first and then try transforming \(x\).

title: Lec 06: Lack of Fit Test and Data Transformation
text:
3.2 Data Transformation: General Rules

Common transformations include:

Logarithmic transformation: \(y' = \log(y)\) or \(x' = \log(x)\)
Square root transformation: \(y' = \sqrt{y}\) or \(x' = \sqrt{x}\)
Reciprocal transformation: \(y' = 1/y\) or \(x' = 1/x\)
Box-Cox transformation: a family of power transformations that includes the above as special cases.

The choice of transformation depends on the specific characteristics of the data and the goals of the analysis.

text:
4.1 Box-Cox Transformation

Box-Cox transformation is defined as: \[
y^{(\lambda)} = \begin{cases}
\frac{y^\lambda - 1}{\lambda}, & \lambda \neq 0 \\
\log(y), & \lambda = 0
\end{cases}
\] E.g., when \(\lambda=0.5\), it is a square root transformation, i.e., \(y'=\sqrt{y}\).
How to find \(\lambda\)? Box-Cox transformation finds the optimal \(\lambda\) by maximizing the log-likelihood function.

\[y_i^{(\lambda)} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i, \quad \epsilon_i \overset{iid}\sim N(0, \sigma^2)\] - The fucntion ``boxcox’’ in MASS package in R can be used to find the optimal \(\lambda\).

title: Lec 06: Lack of Fit Test and Data Transformation

In this example, the optimal value of \(\lambda\) is around 0, which suggests a log transformation on y.

       xlab = expression(lambda),
